name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_SOLIDS_MATCH_MCQ_Q01 - Matching elastic moduli with governing definitions

questiontext.text:
Match the elastic properties listed in List I with their corresponding physical definitions in List II:

List IList II
(A) Young's modulus(I) Ratio of hydraulic stress to volume strain
(B) Shear modulus(II) Ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
(C) Bulk modulus(III) Ratio of tensile or compressive stress to longitudinal strain
(D) Poisson's ratio(IV) Ratio of shearing stress to shearing strain

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Modulus of elasticity is defined by Hooke's law as the ratio of stress to the corresponding strain for small deformations within the proportional limit. The specific modulus depends on the mode of deformation: longitudinal, shear, or volumetric. Lateral strain induced by longitudinal stress is described by Poisson's ratio.

Step 2: Analysis of Young's Modulus
Young's modulus \(Y\) measures the resistance of a solid body to elongation or compression parallel to the applied normal force. It is defined quantitatively as the ratio of tensile (or compressive) stress to longitudinal strain: \(Y = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon} = \frac{F / A}{\Delta L / L}\). Therefore, Young's modulus corresponds to the ratio of tensile or compressive stress to longitudinal strain.

Step 3: Analysis of Shear Modulus
Shear modulus \(G\) (also known as modulus of rigidity) describes the resistance of a body to shape change under tangential deforming forces applied parallel to opposite faces. It is defined as the ratio of tangential (shearing) stress to the resulting shearing strain: \(G = \frac{\sigma_s}{\theta} = \frac{F / A}{\Delta x / L}\). Therefore, shear modulus corresponds to the ratio of shearing stress to shearing strain.

Step 4: Analysis of Bulk Modulus and Poisson's Ratio
Bulk modulus \(B\) measures resistance to uniform volume compression under pressure and is defined as the ratio of hydraulic stress to the resulting volume strain: \(B = -\frac{p}{\Delta V / V}\). Poisson's ratio \(\nu\) describes the simultaneous transverse contraction accompanying longitudinal elongation within the elastic limit and is defined as the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain: \(\nu = \frac{\Delta d / d}{\Delta L / L}\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Matching each term with its definition yields: Young's modulus pairs with ratio of tensile or compressive stress to longitudinal strain; Shear modulus pairs with ratio of shearing stress to shearing strain; Bulk modulus pairs with ratio of hydraulic stress to volume strain; and Poisson's ratio pairs with ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain. This establishes the combination: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_SOLIDS_MATCH_MCQ_Q02 - Matching stress strain curve key points

questiontext.text:
Match the key points and regions of a typical metal stress-strain curve in List I with their physical significance in List II:

List IList II
(A) Proportional limit(I) The point at which the material completely breaks or fractures under load
(B) Yield point(II) The maximum tensile stress that the material can sustain before necking occurs
(C) Ultimate tensile strength(III) The point up to which stress is directly proportional to strain and Hooke's law is obeyed
(D) Fracture point(IV) The elastic limit beyond which the material acquires permanent set and plastic deformation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a standard tensile test of a metal, recording stress against strain produces a characteristic curve. This curve demarcates the proportional elastic region, the elastic limit, the plastic deformation domain, the peak load capacity, and the final failure point.

Step 2: Analysis of the Proportional Limit and Yield Point
The proportional limit represents the boundary of the strictly linear portion of the stress-strain curve from the origin. Up to this point, stress is directly proportional to strain, meaning Hooke's law is obeyed. The yield point (also called the elastic limit) is the point beyond which the material no longer returns to its original dimensions upon unloading; any deformation beyond this point produces a permanent set and plastic deformation.

Step 3: Analysis of Ultimate Tensile Strength and Fracture Point
The ultimate tensile strength is the maximum nominal stress that the material can sustain on the stress-strain curve. Beyond this peak point, localized necking develops and additional strain occurs even with decreasing applied load. The fracture point is the terminal point on the curve where structural separation occurs and the test specimen completely breaks.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Matching each feature with its physical description yields: Proportional limit pairs with the point up to which Hooke's law is obeyed; Yield point pairs with the elastic limit beyond which permanent set occurs; Ultimate tensile strength pairs with the maximum tensile stress sustained before necking; and Fracture point pairs with the point where the material breaks. This establishes the combination: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_SOLIDS_MATCH_MCQ_Q03 - Matching mechanical formulas with physical situations

questiontext.text:
Match the physical situations and phenomena in List I with their governing mathematical expressions in List II:

List IList II
(A) Depression of a rectangular beam loaded at the centre(I) \(u = \frac{1}{2} \times \sigma \times \varepsilon\)
(B) Elastic potential energy per unit volume of a stretched wire(II) \(\delta = \frac{W l^3}{4 b d^3 Y}\)
(C) Shearing strain of a rectangular block under tangential force(III) \(h_{\text{max}} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{limit}}}{\rho g}\)
(D) Maximum allowable height of a mountain on Earth(IV) \(\tan \theta = \frac{\Delta x}{L} \approx \theta\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The mechanical behaviour of solids under stress is governed by rigorous mathematical expressions derived from elastic moduli, equilibrium geometry, and energy conservation.

Step 2: Analysis of Beam Depression and Energy Density
For a horizontal rectangular beam of length \(l\), breadth \(b\), and depth \(d\) supported at its ends and loaded at the centre by a weight \(W\), the sag or depression is given by \(\delta = \frac{W l^3}{4 b d^3 Y}\), where \(Y\) is Young's modulus. For a wire under tensile stress \(\sigma\) and longitudinal strain \(\varepsilon\), the work done during elongation per unit volume is stored as elastic potential energy density \(u = \frac{1}{2} \times \sigma \times \varepsilon\).

Step 3: Analysis of Shearing Strain and Maximum Mountain Height
When a tangential force acts on a face of a cylinder or rectangular block of height \(L\), producing a relative horizontal displacement \(\Delta x\) between opposite faces, the shearing strain is defined as the angle of shear \(\tan \theta = \frac{\Delta x}{L} \approx \theta\). At the base of a mountain of height \(h\) and density \(\rho\), the unbalanced vertical weight creates a lateral shear stress approximately equal to \(h \rho g\). Setting this equal to the critical shear limit of rock \(\sigma_{\text{limit}}\) gives the maximum mountain height \(h_{\text{max}} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{limit}}}{\rho g}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Matching each situation with its mathematical expression yields: Depression of a rectangular beam pairs with \(\frac{W l^3}{4 b d^3 Y}\); Elastic potential energy density pairs with \(\frac{1}{2} \sigma \varepsilon\); Shearing strain pairs with \(\frac{\Delta x}{L} \approx \theta\); and Maximum mountain height pairs with \(\frac{\sigma_{\text{limit}}}{\rho g}\). This establishes the combination: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.
